title: Observe Correct Handling Procedures of Condemned Material

lessons.title: What condemned material is and why control matters
lessons.html:
Condemned material

Condemned material is any carcass, part or offal that has been judged unfit for human consumption. It includes whole carcasses with generalised disease, livers with fluke or abscesses, lungs with pneumonia, trimmings of bruises and contamination, and parts with measles or hydatid cysts. Under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 condemned material must never enter the human food chain.

Why strict control is needed

  • Food safety: condemned meat can carry bacteria, parasites and residues that make people ill.
  • Disease control: condemned offal fed to dogs spreads tapeworms that cause hydatid cysts and measles. Material from animals with diseases like anthrax or tuberculosis can spread the disease to people and animals.
  • Theft and fraud: condemned meat has value to criminals who sell it illegally. Control prevents it from being stolen and sold.
  • Trust: buyers and the public trust the inspection mark only if condemned meat is controlled.

The meat examiner's role

The meat examiner makes the judgement and then observes that the abattoir handles the material correctly from the moment it is condemned until it leaves the site or is destroyed. You do not have to carry the material yourself, but you must see that the procedure is followed and record the quantities.

Special risks

If anthrax is suspected, the carcass must not be opened further, moved through the hall or sent to normal disposal. Stop, isolate the area and call the veterinarian immediately; disposal will be under the veterinarian's instruction. Wear gloves when handling condemned material and wash hands and arms afterwards.

lessons.title: Marking, containers and the route out
lessons.html:
From the line to disposal

Every abattoir must have a written procedure for condemned material. Watch that each step is followed.

1. Identify and mark

Condemned carcasses and parts are clearly marked with the condemned mark or stained with a coloured dye (denaturant) as the procedure requires. Staining makes the meat obviously unfit so it cannot be sold.

2. Containers

  • Use clearly labelled containers or bins kept only for condemned material, often in a specific colour.
  • Containers should be leak-proof and have lids.
  • They must never be used for edible products, and edible product containers must never be used for condemned material.

3. Removal from the hall

Condemned material is removed regularly, through a chute or route that does not cross clean areas or passed meat. It must not stand next to passed carcasses or in the chiller with them.

4. Storage

The condemned material room or container is lockable and kept locked. Only authorised people have keys. The area is cleaned regularly and kept free of flies and rodents.

5. Disposal

Material goes to an approved method, such as a rendering plant, incinerator or approved burial site, according to the abattoir's permit and the veterinarian's instructions. Each removal is recorded.

Records

Record the date, carcass numbers, type and weight or number of parts condemned, and how they were disposed of. Compare the amount condemned on the line with the amount removed. A big difference may mean material is going missing.

Key points

  • Condemned material must never enter the human food chain.
  • Mark or stain condemned material so it cannot be sold.
  • Use labelled, leak-proof containers kept only for condemned material.
  • Keep the condemned room locked and the route separate from clean areas.
  • Record quantities and disposal, and compare them to detect losses.

quiz.question: Why is condemned material stained with a coloured dye?

options.text: To make it obviously unfit so it cannot be sold

quiz.question: How does feeding condemned offal to dogs spread disease?

options.text: It spreads tapeworms that cause hydatid cysts and measles
It causes foot rot in sheep
It has no effect on disease

quiz.question: What should happen to the condemned material room?

options.text: It should be left open for easy access
It should be inside the chiller
It should be locked, with only authorised people holding keys
It should be next to the dispatch bay

quiz.question: If anthrax is suspected, what must happen to the carcass?

options.text: Cut it up and send it to rendering as normal
Move it quickly through the hall to the bins
Do not open it further; isolate the area and call the veterinarian

quiz.question: Why compare the amount condemned on the line with the amount removed?

options.text: To detect material that may be going missing
